add_questions: When did the high iodine exposure begin?
Any recent CT scans or angiography with contrast?
Are you taking any kelp, seaweed, or iodine supplements?
If on amiodarone: Duration of use? Any plans to continue?
Any symptoms that started shortly after the exposure?
add_workup: TSH, free T4, total T3 (baseline thyroid function)
24-hour urinary iodine excretion (if clinically indicated)
Thyroid antibodies (TPO, TSI) to distinguish from Graves' disease
Thyroid ultrasound with Doppler (assess vascularity)
Consider thyroid uptake scan (typically low in iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis)
add_red_flags: Severe tachycardia or new atrial fibrillation
Signs of thyroid storm (fever, altered mental status, severe agitation)
Pregnancy (iodine excess can affect fetal thyroid)
Pre-existing cardiac disease with new arrhythmias
referral_notes: Consider endocrinology referral for: severe symptoms, cardiac complications, pregnancy, or diagnostic uncertainty
Cardiology consultation if new or worsening arrhythmia
If amiodarone-induced: coordinate with prescribing cardiologist regarding medication continuation
effects.reasoning: Excess iodine intake can trigger thyrotoxicosis in susceptible individuals, particularly those with underlying thyroid autonomy or nodular disease. The Jod-Basedow phenomenon describes iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, most common in iodine-deficient populations exposed to iodine load. Amiodarone contains 37% iodine by weight and can cause both hyper- and hypothyroidism. Diagnosis requires correlation of exposure history with thyroid function tests and imaging. Treatment may require beta-blockers, thionamides, and removal of iodine source when possible.
clinical_pearls: Jod-Basedow is more common in areas with chronic iodine deficiency
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis has two types: Type 1 (iodine excess) and Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis)
Thyroid uptake scan shows low uptake in iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis (vs. high in Graves')
Some patients may require temporary glucocorticoids if destructive thyroiditis is present

triggers.description: Combined high iodine from multiple sources

add_to_differential: Wolff-Chaikoff effect (transient hypothyroidism from iodine excess)
add_questions: How long have you been consuming high amounts of iodine?
Any family history of thyroid disease?
Have you noticed changes in thyroid size or symptoms?
Any difficulty swallowing or breathing?

Thyroid ultrasound (assess goiter size, nodules, vascularity)
If nodules >1cm: Consider FNA biopsy per ATA guidelines
Urinary iodine if diagnosis uncertain
Thyroid antibodies if autoimmune component suspected

ENT/Surgery referral if compressive symptoms or malignancy concern
effects.reasoning: Chronic iodine excess can lead to goiter formation and thyroid dysfunction. The Wolff-Chaikoff effect describes temporary inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis with acute iodine loads. In individuals with underlying thyroid abnormalities, excess iodine may unmask or worsen goiter or nodular disease. Management focuses on identifying and modifying iodine sources, monitoring thyroid function, and evaluating for malignancy risk per established guidelines.
clinical_pearls: Most healthy individuals can tolerate high iodine intake due to autoregulation
Iodine-induced goiter is more common in those with pre-existing thyroid autonomy
Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) for iodine is 1,100 mcg/day for adults
Kelp supplements can contain highly variable and excessive iodine amounts

triggers.description: Frequent raw or undercooked fish consumption

add_questions: What type of fish was consumed and when?
Where was the fish sourced from (restaurant, home, region)?
Any others who ate the same fish with similar symptoms?
Timing of symptom onset after fish consumption?
Any neurologic symptoms (paresthesias, temperature reversal)?

Stool ova and parasites x3 (if parasitic infection suspected)
Serum IgE to Anisakis (if allergic symptoms)
CBC with differential (eosinophilia may suggest parasitic infection)
Consider endoscopy if severe abdominal pain and negative initial workup
add_red_flags: Neurologic symptoms (suggest ciguatera or severe scombroid)
referral_notes: Consider gastroenterology referral if symptoms persist or complications develop
Infectious disease consultation for severe or atypical presentations
Allergy/immunology if recurrent reactions to seafood
effects.reasoning: Raw or undercooked fish consumption carries risk of parasitic and bacterial infections as well as toxin-mediated illnesses. Anisakis species (roundworms) can cause acute gastric symptoms and allergic reactions. Scombroid poisoning results from histamine in improperly stored fish (tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi) and presents with flushing and GI symptoms. Ciguatera toxin affects large reef fish and causes distinctive GI and neurologic symptoms. Vibrio species are common in raw shellfish and fish from warm coastal waters. Diagnosis requires careful exposure history and targeted testing.
clinical_pearls: Anisakis can be seen on endoscopy as a whitish worm embedded in gastric mucosa
Scombroid poisoning mimics allergic reaction but is histamine toxicity (antihistamines help)
Ciguatera's pathognomonic feature is 'temperature reversal' (cold feels hot and vice versa)
Most cases are self-limited; treatment is supportive
Prevention: fish should be frozen to -20°C for 7 days to kill Anisakis larvae

rules.name: Travel to South Asia - Fever Evaluation

add_to_differential: Malaria (primarily P. vivax in South Asia)
add_questions: Specific countries visited? Rural vs urban areas?
Mosquito bite prevention measures used?
Malaria prophylaxis taken? Which medication and compliance?
Vaccination history (typhoid, hepatitis A, others)?
Consumed street food, raw vegetables, or unfiltered water?
Duration of travel and timing of fever onset?
Any sick contacts during travel?
Animal exposures?
add_workup: Thick and thin blood smears for malaria (repeat q12-24h x3 if negative)
Malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT)
Blood cultures (for typhoid and other bacteremia)
CBC with differential (thrombocytopenia common in malaria and dengue)
Liver enzymes (elevated in many tropical infections)
Dengue NS1 antigen and IgM/IgG serology
Typhoid IgM serology or Widal test (low sensitivity)
Urinalysis and urine culture
CXR if respiratory symptoms or prolonged fever (TB screening)
add_red_flags: Jaundice with fever (severe malaria, hepatitis, leptospirosis)
referral_notes: URGENT infectious disease consultation recommended for febrile returned traveler
Consider ED evaluation if severe symptoms, altered mental status, or high malaria risk
Admit if malaria confirmed or severe symptoms regardless of etiology
Isolate if hemorrhagic fever or highly contagious pathogen suspected
effects.reasoning: Fever in returned travelers from South Asia requires systematic evaluation for region-specific pathogens. Malaria is a medical emergency and must be ruled out urgently in any febrile traveler from endemic areas. South Asia has high burden of typhoid fever, dengue, and other mosquito-borne diseases. Timing of symptom onset relative to travel helps narrow differential: malaria typically presents within weeks, typhoid in 1-3 weeks, dengue in 4-7 days. Empiric treatment should not delay diagnostic testing. Many conditions require specific antimicrobials (e.g., artemisinin-based therapy for malaria, fluoroquinolones or ceftriaxone for typhoid in regions with resistance).
clinical_pearls: Malaria can present weeks to months after travel; P. vivax can have delayed onset
Negative initial malaria smear does NOT exclude malaria; repeat testing essential
Dengue: warning signs include abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy
Typhoid: 'step-ladder' fever pattern, relative bradycardia, rose spots are classic but not always present
Always ask about pre-travel vaccines and malaria prophylaxis compliance
Drug-resistant typhoid and malaria are increasing in South Asia

rules.name: Travel to Sub-Saharan Africa - Fever Evaluation

add_questions: Specific countries and regions visited?
Safari or rural exposure? Freshwater swimming?
Yellow fever vaccination status?
Malaria prophylaxis used and compliance?
Tick bites or insect exposures?
Sexual contacts or blood exposure?
Bushmeat consumption or contact with wild animals?
Any known Ebola or other outbreak in travel region?
add_workup: STAT malaria smears and RDT (repeat q12-24h x3) - P. falciparum can be rapidly fatal
Blood cultures for typhoid and bacteremia
CBC with differential (thrombocytopenia, anemia in malaria)
Comprehensive metabolic panel (renal function, liver enzymes)
Dengue serology and NS1 antigen
HIV 4th generation Ag/Ab test
Rickettsial serology if eschar or severe headache
Viral hemorrhagic fever testing if high-risk exposure and severe symptoms (in isolation)
Schistosomiasis serology if freshwater exposure and eosinophilia
add_red_flags: HIGH PRIORITY: Any concern for viral hemorrhagic fever (Ebola, Marburg, Lassa) - ISOLATE IMMEDIATELY
Severe malaria signs: altered mental status, seizures, severe anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema
referral_notes: IMMEDIATE infectious disease consultation required
ED evaluation strongly recommended - do not delay
Hospital admission likely needed for workup and monitoring
Contact infection control and public health if viral hemorrhagic fever suspected
Strict isolation precautions if hemorrhagic fever in differential
effects.reasoning: Fever in travelers from Sub-Saharan Africa is a medical emergency requiring urgent evaluation. P. falciparum malaria predominates and can progress to severe disease and death within hours if untreated. Unlike other regions, Africa has higher risk of viral hemorrhagic fevers, though rare. HIV seroconversion illness should be considered in those with sexual exposure. Schistosomiasis can cause acute febrile illness (Katayama fever) 2-8 weeks after freshwater exposure. Yellow fever vaccination is required for many African countries, and disease can occur in unvaccinated travelers. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment are critical for malaria and bacterial infections. Any suspicion of viral hemorrhagic fever requires immediate isolation and public health notification.
clinical_pearls: P. falciparum malaria can be rapidly fatal; parasitemia >5% or any organ dysfunction = severe malaria
Severe malaria requires IV artesunate (preferred) or quinidine + ICU care
African tick bite fever: look for eschar (black necrotic lesion at tick bite site)
Viral hemorrhagic fevers: extremely rare but high mortality; fever + bleeding + travel to outbreak area = isolation
Katayama fever: acute schistosomiasis presents with fever, urticaria, eosinophilia 2-8 weeks post-exposure
Always verify yellow fever vaccination status in Africa travelers

triggers.description: Travel to histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis endemic area

add_to_differential: Coccidioidomycosis (Valley Fever) - if southwestern US or Central/South America
add_questions: Exposure to caves, bat or bird droppings?
Construction, excavation, or soil disturbance activities?
Duration in endemic area?
Immunocompromised status (HIV, immunosuppressants)?
Chronic symptoms vs acute presentation?
add_workup: Fungal blood cultures (Histoplasma, Coccidioides)
Urine Histoplasma antigen
Serum Coccidioides IgM and IgG
Fungal stains and cultures of sputum
Chest CT (may show cavitation, nodules, mediastinal lymphadenopathy)
HIV testing
Tuberculin skin test or IGRA
add_red_flags: Immunocompromised patient (higher risk of disseminated disease)
referral_notes: Consider infectious disease consultation for diagnostic guidance and treatment
Pulmonology referral if bronchoscopy needed for diagnosis
Immunocompromised patients require aggressive workup and treatment
effects.reasoning: Endemic mycoses should be considered in patients with pneumonia and exposure to specific geographic regions. Histoplasmosis is endemic in Ohio/Mississippi River valleys and parts of Central/South America, associated with bat/bird droppings. Coccidioidomycosis (Valley Fever) occurs in southwestern US and parts of Mexico/Central/South America. These infections can range from asymptomatic to severe disseminated disease, especially in immunocompromised hosts. Diagnosis requires high index of suspicion and specialized testing.
clinical_pearls: Most endemic fungal infections are mild and self-limited in immunocompetent hosts
Disseminated disease more common in HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients, immunosuppressants
Histoplasmosis: can cause acute pulmonary infection or chronic cavitary disease
Valley Fever: classic 'desert rheumatism' triad = fever, rash, arthralgias
Treatment: itraconazole for mild-moderate, amphotericin B for severe disease

add_to_differential: Biotin interference causing falsely abnormal thyroid tests
Pseudohyperthyroidism (falsely elevated T4/T3, falsely low TSH)
May also affect troponin, BNP, and other immunoassays
add_questions: What dose of biotin are you taking daily?
When did you start the supplement?
When was the last dose before blood draw?
Are you taking 'hair, skin, and nails' supplements? (often contain biotin)
Any cardiac symptoms or concerns?
add_workup: Hold biotin for 48-72 hours before repeating labs
Repeat thyroid function tests after biotin washout
If urgent: Request biotin-interference-resistant assay
Check troponin and BNP if cardiac concerns (also affected by biotin)
add_red_flags: Do NOT make clinical decisions based on potentially biotin-interfered results
Ensure biotin status documented before starting therapy
Patient may falsely appear hyperthyroid or have masked hypothyroidism
referral_notes: Counsel patient to discontinue biotin at least 48 hours before any laboratory testing
Endocrinology referral if thyroid dysfunction confirmed after biotin washout
effects.reasoning: High-dose biotin (>1mg daily) can cause significant interference with laboratory immunoassays that use biotin-streptavidin technology. For thyroid tests, biotin typically causes falsely elevated T4 and T3 with falsely suppressed TSH, mimicking hyperthyroidism. This can lead to misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment. Biotin is increasingly common in over-the-counter supplements for hair, skin, and nails. The FDA issued a safety alert in 2019 warning about biotin interference. Diagnosis requires clinical suspicion and repeat testing after biotin washout (48-72 hours).
clinical_pearls: Biotin doses >1mg can interfere; some supplements contain 5-10mg or more
Interference pattern: TSH low, T4/T3 high (looks like hyperthyroidism)
Also affects: troponin (falsely low), BNP (falsely low), testosterone, others
48-72 hour washout is sufficient for most assays
Always ask about supplements before interpreting discordant labs

add_to_differential: E. coli O157:H7 (hemolytic uremic syndrome risk)
Brucellosis (if recent travel or occupational exposure)
add_questions: What type of unpasteurized dairy (milk, cheese, etc.)?
Source of the dairy (farm, store, region)?
When was it consumed?
Anyone else ill with similar symptoms?
Any fever, bloody diarrhea, or severe abdominal pain?
Pregnant or immunocompromised?
add_workup: Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli O157
Stool Shiga toxin assay (for E. coli O157:H7)
CBC (watch for thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia if HUS suspected)
BMP and creatinine (renal function if HUS concern)
Blood cultures if fever/systemic symptoms (Listeria, Salmonella)
Brucella serology if risk factors present
add_red_flags: Bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramps (E. coli O157:H7)
Signs of hemolytic uremic syndrome: decreased urine output, pallor, petechiae
referral_notes: Report to public health if E. coli O157, Listeria, or outbreak suspected
Nephrology consultation if HUS develops
Infectious disease consultation for Brucella or complicated cases
OB consultation if pregnant patient with Listeria concern
effects.reasoning: Unpasteurized dairy products can harbor numerous foodborne pathogens eliminated by pasteurization. E. coli O157:H7 can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a life-threatening complication particularly in children. Listeria monocytogenes can cause severe infection in pregnant women, elderly, and immunocompromised, with high risk of fetal loss or neonatal infection. Campylobacter and Salmonella cause acute gastroenteritis. Brucellosis should be considered in those with occupational exposure or travel to endemic areas. Most cases are self-limited but severe cases or high-risk patients may require antibiotics. Antibiotic use in E. coli O157:H7 is controversial and may increase HUS risk.
clinical_pearls: Do NOT use antibiotics if E. coli O157:H7 suspected (may increase HUS risk)
Listeria: treat with ampicillin + gentamicin in severe cases
HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury
Raw milk outbreaks are increasing; CDC recommends avoiding unpasteurized dairy
Pregnant women should strictly avoid raw dairy due to Listeria risk

add_to_differential: Carbon monoxide exposure (if also combustion exposure)
add_questions: What is your occupation and specific exposures?
Use of personal protective equipment?
Other workers with similar symptoms?
Symptoms worse at work, improve on days off?
Other neurologic symptoms: memory, mood, tremor, paresthesias?
GI symptoms (common in lead and arsenic poisoning)?
Home exposures (old paint, contaminated water)?
add_workup: Blood lead level (if lead exposure)
24-hour urine heavy metal screen
CBC (lead causes anemia with basophilic stippling)
Comprehensive metabolic panel (renal function)
Nerve conduction studies if peripheral neuropathy symptoms
Consider occupational medicine or toxicology consultation
add_red_flags: Acute severe symptoms suggesting high-level exposure
referral_notes: Occupational medicine referral for workplace assessment
Toxicology consultation for chelation therapy consideration
Report to OSHA if workplace hazard identified
Neurology referral if persistent symptoms or neuropathy
effects.reasoning: Occupational exposures to heavy metals and solvents can cause chronic headaches along with other neurologic symptoms. Lead poisoning presents with headaches, abdominal pain, anemia, and peripheral neuropathy. Mercury can cause tremor, cognitive impairment, and mood changes. Arsenic causes peripheral neuropathy and GI symptoms. Carbon monoxide causes headaches, confusion, and can be fatal. Diagnosis requires occupational history, exposure assessment, and targeted laboratory testing. Treatment includes removal from exposure and, in some cases, chelation therapy. Workplace evaluation is critical to prevent further cases.
clinical_pearls: Lead: 'lead line' on gingiva, basophilic stippling on blood smear, wrist/foot drop
Mercury: 'Mad Hatter syndrome' - tremor, erethism (personality change)
Arsenic: 'Mees lines' on nails, hyperpigmentation, peripheral neuropathy
CO: 'cherry red' skin is rare; carboxyhemoglobin level diagnostic
Chelation therapy indicated for symptomatic lead poisoning or very high levels

CBC (anemia from GI bleeding or heavy metal toxicity)
Review supplement ingredients for known GI effects
Consider heavy metal screen if imported/unregulated supplements
Medication reconciliation for drug-herb interactions

Hepatology referral if significant liver enzyme elevation
Recommend stopping herbal supplements and reassessing
effects.reasoning: Many herbal supplements can cause GI side effects including diarrhea. Common culprits include senna, cascara sagrada, aloe vera, and various 'detox' or 'cleanse' products. Some herbs interact with medications affecting GI motility. Additionally, imported or unregulated supplements may be contaminated with heavy metals or adulterants. Some traditional medicines contain deliberately added pharmaceuticals. Herbal hepatotoxicity can cause cholestatic changes affecting digestion. Diagnosis requires detailed supplement history and trial of discontinuation. Many cases resolve with stopping the offending agent.
clinical_pearls: Senna, cascara, aloe: stimulant laxatives causing cramping and diarrhea
St. John's Wort: induces CYP450, numerous drug interactions
Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese Medicine products: risk of heavy metal contamination
Kava, germander, comfrey: hepatotoxic
Many patients don't report supplements unless specifically asked

triggers.description: Uses well water as primary water source

add_to_differential: Hepatitis A (fecal-oral transmission from contaminated water)
Heavy metal toxicity (arsenic, lead in groundwater)
add_questions: Well water tested recently? When and results?
Well maintenance and depth?
Proximity to septic systems, agricultural runoff, or industrial sites?
Others in household affected?
Hepatitis vaccination status?
Use water filter? Type?
Flooding or heavy rain recently?
add_workup: Hepatitis A IgM (acute infection)
Hepatitis E IgM and PCR
Comprehensive hepatic panel
Well water testing: bacterial (coliforms, E. coli), chemical (nitrates, heavy metals)
Heavy metal screen if chronic exposure suspected
referral_notes: Report to local health department if hepatitis A or contaminated well suspected
Environmental health assessment of well water needed
Gastroenterology/hepatology for significant hepatitis
Recommend immediate cessation of well water use until tested
effects.reasoning: Private well water can be contaminated with infectious agents and chemicals, unlike treated municipal water. Hepatitis A and E can be transmitted via fecally contaminated water. Agricultural runoff may introduce bacterial pathogens. Heavy metals (arsenic, lead) and nitrates from fertilizers can leach into groundwater, causing chronic toxicity. Wells should be tested annually for bacteria and every 3-5 years for chemicals. Contamination risk increases after flooding, near septic systems, or in agricultural areas. Diagnosis requires water testing and appropriate serologic or toxicologic studies.
clinical_pearls: EPA does not regulate private wells; owner's responsibility to test
Hepatitis E genotype 3 is emerging in US, associated with contaminated water and undercooked pork
Arsenic in groundwater: chronic exposure causes hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, skin changes, cancer risk
Nitrates >10 ppm unsafe for infants (methemoglobinemia)
Boiling water does NOT remove chemical contaminants or heavy metals

triggers.description: Regular swimming in natural water sources

add_to_differential: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis (Naegleria fowleri) - rare but rapidly fatal
add_questions: What type of water (lake, river, pond, hot spring)?
Geographic location of water exposure?
Recent warm weather? Water temperature?
Water activities: diving, jumping, water sports (forcing water up nose)?
Timing: symptoms within 1-9 days of exposure?
Headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, seizures?
Loss of smell or taste?
add_workup: URGENT: LP with CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture)
CSF: bacterial culture, viral PCR panel (HSV, enterovirus)
CSF: wet mount for amoeba (requires immediate fresh specimen examination)
CSF: Naegleria PCR if available (send to CDC if suspected)
Brain MRI with contrast (may show hemorrhagic changes in Naegleria)
Blood cultures
Leptospira serology and PCR
add_red_flags: CRITICAL: Rapidly progressive meningoencephalitis in recent freshwater swimmer = Naegleria until proven otherwise
Anosmia (loss of smell) with recent warm freshwater exposure
referral_notes: IMMEDIATE neurology and infectious disease consultation
ICU admission for any CNS infection
If Naegleria suspected: contact CDC Emergency Operations Center immediately (770-488-7100)
Naegleria treatment: IV and intrathecal/intraventricular amphotericin B + miltefosine + others
effects.reasoning: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) caused by Naegleria fowleri is a rare but almost universally fatal infection. The amoeba enters through the nose during swimming/diving in warm freshwater and migrates to the brain. PAM typically presents 1-9 days after exposure with severe frontal headache, fever, nausea, vomiting, progressing rapidly to altered mental status, seizures, and coma. Mortality is >97% but early diagnosis and aggressive treatment may be lifesaving. CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose, mimicking bacterial meningitis. Diagnosis requires high index of suspicion and immediate fresh CSF examination for motile trophozoites. Leptospirosis can occur after freshwater exposure and may have CNS involvement.
clinical_pearls: Naegleria: 'brain-eating amoeba' - infects via nose, not from swallowing water
Most cases in southern US during summer; warm water <30°C (86°F)
Loss of smell (anosmia) is early sign - amoeba destroys olfactory neuroepithelium
CSF: must examine fresh, warm specimen immediately - amoeba stops moving when cooled
Survival requires early diagnosis and multimodal therapy including miltefosine (investigational)
Leptospirosis: ask about animal exposure (rats), jaundice, conjunctival suffusion
